module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Fibonacci transform satisfying $|a(n)| = F(n+1)$

The sequence $a(n)$ satisfies the linear recurrence relation:
$$a(n) = 3a(n-1) - 4a(n-2) + 2a(n-3) - a(n-4)$$
with initial terms $a(0)=0, a(1)=1, a(2)=1, a(3)=0$.
The sequence takes values in $\mathbb{Z}$.

*References:*
- [A103311](https://oeis.org/A103311)
- [arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763) *Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search* by George Tsoukalas et al.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace OeisA103311


/--
The sequence $a(n)$ satisfies the linear recurrence relation:
$$a(n) = 3a(n-1) - 4a(n-2) + 2a(n-3) - a(n-4)$$
with initial terms $a(0)=0, a(1)=1, a(2)=1, a(3)=0$.
The sequence takes values in $\mathbb{Z}$.
-/
def a : ℕ → ℤ
| 0 => 0
| 1 => 1
| 2 => 1
| 3 => 0
| n + 4 => 3 * a (n + 3) - 4 * a (n + 2) + 2 * a (n + 1) - a n


@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_0 : a 0 = 0 := by rfl

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_1 : a 1 = 1 := by rfl

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_2 : a 2 = 1 := by rfl

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_3 : a 3 = 0 := by rfl

@[category test, AMS 11]
lemma a_4 : a 4 = -2 := by rfl


/--
Fibonacci transform satisfying $|a(n)| = F(n+1)$.

Conjecture: all elements in absolute value are Fibonacci numbers.

A formal proof has been found with the methods described in
[arxiv/2605.22763](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/a32396489dcb8f86c3549b93aa358ac6a10a3a1f/FormalConjectures/OEIS/103311.wip.lean#L218"]
theorem a_abs_eq_fib (n : ℕ) : ∃ m : ℕ, Int.natAbs (a n) = Nat.fib m := by
    sorry

end OeisA103311

findings.description: The docstring of `a_abs_eq_fib` opens with "Fibonacci transform satisfying $|a(n)| = F(n+1)$." The module docstring title repeats this ("# Fibonacci transform satisfying $|a(n)| = F(n+1)$"). This identity is false for the sequence the file defines. It fails at n = 0 (|a(0)| = 0 ≠ 1 = F(1)), at n = 2 (1 vs F(3) = 2) and at n = 3 (a(3) = 0 vs F(4) = 3). Checked in Lean: `¬ ∀ n, Int.natAbs (a n) = Nat.fib (n + 1)` compiles, and among n < 1000 the identity holds only at n = 1. It fails under any Fibonacci indexing, since F(n+1) ≥ 1 while a(5k+3) = 0. Neither the Lean statement (`∃ m, Int.natAbs (a n) = Nat.fib m`) nor the OEIS entry makes this claim. The theorem itself is faithful, so the mathematics is intact; only the prose is wrong. The correct pattern (proved in my scratch file) is: a(5k) = (−1)^k F(5k), a(5k+1) = a(5k+2) = (−1)^k F(5k+1), a(5k+3) = 0, a(5k+4) = −(−1)^k F(5k+3).
findings.source_evidence: OEIS A103311 (https://oeis.org/A103311, read via web.archive.org snapshot 20260904141626): name "A transform of the Fibonacci numbers."; data "0, 1, 1, 0, -2, -5, -8, -8, 0, 21, 55, 89, 89, 0, -233, ..."; comment "Conjecture: all elements in absolute value are Fibonacci numbers." The proof comment describes "a period-5 pattern ... signed Fibonacci terms (-1)^k * fib(...)". Nowhere does the entry claim |a(n)| = F(n+1).
findings.suggested_fix: Replace "Fibonacci transform satisfying $|a(n)| = F(n+1)$" in the module title and in the theorem docstring with the OEIS name, e.g. "# A transform of the Fibonacci numbers". Alternatively use "Every term of A103311 is, in absolute value, a Fibonacci number". If a closed form is wanted, give the period-5 pattern: $|a(5k)| = F(5k)$, $|a(5k+1)| = |a(5k+2)| = F(5k+1)$, $a(5k+3) = 0$, $|a(5k+4)| = F(5k+3)$.

reformulations.difference: OEIS defines A103311 by a construction: apply the Chebyshev transform (1/(1+x^2), x/(1+x^2)), then the binomial involution (1/(1-x), -x/(1-x)), as Riordan arrays, to -F(n). The Lean definition instead uses the order-4 recurrence a(n+4) = 3a(n+3) - 4a(n+2) + 2a(n+1) - a(n) with a(0..3) = 0, 1, 1, 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Composing the Riordan arrays gives the g.f. (1/(1-x)) G(-x/(1-x)), where G(y) = (1/(1+y^2)) F(y/(1+y^2)) and F(y) = -y/(1-y-y^2). Substituting Q = 1-2x+2x^2, this simplifies to x(1-x)^2/(Q^2 + x(1-x)Q - x^2(1-x)^2) = x(1-x)^2/(1-3x+4x^2-2x^3+x^4). That is the OEIS g.f. Its coefficients satisfy exactly this recurrence for n ≥ 4, since the numerator has degree 3, and have initial terms 0, 1, 1, 0. Checked in Lean by #eval: the explicit transform sums Σ_j (-1)^j C(n,j) Σ_i (-1)^i C(j-i,i)(-F(j-2i)) equal the recurrence for n < 60, and the recurrence reproduces all 4789 b-file terms.

review.notes: The Lean statement of `a_abs_eq_fib`, `∀ n, ∃ m, (a n).natAbs = Nat.fib m`, is exactly the OEIS conjecture ("all elements in absolute value are Fibonacci numbers"). It counts 0 = F(0) as a Fibonacci number, which the conjecture needs because a(5k+3) = 0; this matches A000045. I proved the statement against this commit in /workspace/review/proof.lean, using the period-5 pattern and a parity split plus linarith; `#print axioms` shows only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. So the `research solved` tag agrees with the OEIS record that the conjecture was proved by the Tsoukalas et al. agent in May 2026, and Adamczewski (arXiv:2608.11941) independently proved it. The AlphaProof Nexus Lean file linked from OEIS proves the same statement for a byte-identical definition of `a`. I did not open the `formal_proof` URL itself, because it points into a GitHub fork of formal-conjectures (mo271/formal-conjectures), which I treated as off-limits. The claim that a formal proof exists is confirmed by the two proofs above. The test lemmas a_0 through a_4 match the OEIS data. The only defect is the false formula |a(n)| = F(n+1) in the module title and theorem docstring. It is reported once, under the theorem, and covers both places.
